newsitem.title: UK: Britain dismayed by Chinese plan for HK laws. [CORRECTED 14:27 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Britain dismayed by Chinese plan for HK laws. [CORRECTED 14:27 GMT]

text.p: Britain said on Monday it was "dismayed" by China's plan to dilute Hong Kong's bill of rights and replace other key pieces of legislation when it takes over sovereignty at the end of June.

But the Foreign Office said it welcomed an assurance by post-colonial leader Tung Chee-hwa that new legislation would be the subject of public consultation before it was brought in. The Standing Committee of China's parliament, the National People's Congress, approved a plan on Sunday night to amend 25 pieces of Hong Kong legislation.
As well as amending the bill of rights, this would mean replacing laws on the formation of political parties and freedom of association in the territory of 6.4 million people.

A Foreign Office statement said Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind had made it clear to his Chinese opposite number, Qian Qichen, earlier this month that proposals to amend the Hong Kong laws were "unnecessary and unjustified".

"We are dismayed that the Chinese government is going ahead despite the opposition across almost the entire political spectrum in Hong Kong," it said. (Corrects to add dropped words "despite the opposition")
But it added: "The Chief Executive designate (Tung) has pledged that new legislation in this area will be the subject of public consultations in Hong Kong. We welcome this approach."

It said new laws should reflect both the expressed wishes of Hong Kong's people and the provisions of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), a United Nations charter on human rights.
The statement noted that the ICCPR would continue to apply to Hong Kong even after the handover of sovereignty.
